112007.etyen:
Compound of bunn (“bottom, base”) + stokk (“log, timber”), literally “bottom timber”.
The first element bunn is from Danish bund (“bottom”), from Old Danish botn (“bottom”), from Proto-Germanic *butmaz (“bottom, foundation”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰudʰmḗn (“bottom”).
The second element stokk is from Old Norse stokkr (“log, beam”), from Proto-Germanic *stukkaz (“stick, beam, post”). The Proto-Germanic word is probably derived from *stikaną (“to stick, stab”), ultimately from *(s)teyg- (“to be sharp; stab, pierce”), although an alternative derivation from *(s)tewg- (“to push, hit”) has also

The Greek verb is formed from εὐαγγέλιον (euangélion, “good news, gospel”) and -ίζω (-ízō, “verb-forming suffix”).
The εὐ- (eu-, “good, well”) element continues Proto-Hellenic *ehu- (“good”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁su- (“good”); the deeper origin of the ἄγγελος (ángelos, “messenger”) element is uncertain.

Internationalism, based on French Mali, ultimately continuing the name of the medieval Mali Empire. Medieval Arabic sources record forms corresponding to Mali, while Manding tradition uses forms such as Mande, Manden and Manding for the empire's core region and political tradition. The deeper origin and exact relationship between these forms are unknown.

1001095.etyen: From farke (“to roam, wander about”) + -ing (“action/result-forming noun suffix”). The verb farke (“to roam, wander about”) is a denominal derivative of fark (“vagrant, rogue”). The noun fark is derived from Old Norse Old Norse farri (“vagrant, vagabond”), possibly through or under the influence of farre (“vagrant, wanderer”); fark has also been explained as a diminutive formation of farre. Old Norse farri is derived from fara (“to go, travel”), from Proto-Germanic *faraną (“to go, travel”), ultimately from the Proto-Indo-European root *per- (“to go through; carry forth, fare”).
